extractor.note: source_sha256 is the LF digest from corpus.json (CRLF checkout; a local validate reports a false staleness). Retrieval by predecessor name (Husserl, Heidegger, Descartes, Kant, Henry, Derrida, Nietzsche, Levinas, Hegel, Leibniz and others) with a relational word, then targeted reading of the sections that carry each chapter's verdict. Three voices are recorded and each claim names its own: Marion's engagements; Heidegger's with Husserl and Descartes as Marion reconstructs them; Husserl's with Kant and Descartes as Marion reports them. primary_locator gives Marion's chapter and section. Top-up 2026-11-02: II.1, II.6-7 and IV.1-3 read in full for Heidegger (engagements 023-036), with the Heidegger-Husserl voice where those sections carry it; Beaufret recorded where IV.3 argues against him; the Foreword's credit to Franck recorded; Freud, Kern, Kojève, Lacan, Mohanty and Picht searched and not found.

coverage_note: The commentary covers the Foreword, 'Phenomenology as such' and chapters I-IV. Read in full: Foreword, I.3, I.7, II.1, II.6-7, IV.1-3, IV.7 (closing pages). Elsewhere read at the sentences naming a predecessor together with a relational word, plus targeted context in I.5-6, II.2-5, III.2-7 and IV.4-6. Heidegger and Husserl are recorded by each chapter's principal moves, not exhaustively. Passing mentions (Levinas, Ricœur, Leibniz, Spinoza, Malebranche, Pascal, Hegel on the This, Tugendhat, Granel, Courtine; Vail and Salus in IV.3, named alongside Beaufret) are not recorded.

engagements.claim: Marion names Michel Henry in the Foreword; Henry's material phenomenology had already detached manifestation from intuition and from the world's horizon, and Marion's attempt to reduce beyond the question of being borrows that gesture while departing from Henry's answer.
engagements.quote: The last name, Michel Henry, is the philosophically loaded one: Henry's material phenomenology had already detached manifestation from intuition and from the world's horizon, and Marion's eventual attempt to reduce beyond the question of being borrows that gesture even where it departs from Henry's answer.

engagements.claim: Husserl's breakthrough, as Marion reads it, takes over intuition and enlarges it against its Kantian sense, transgressing the finitude for which intuition can only be sensuous, so that the categorial concept itself is given.
engagements.quote: The enlargement of intuition is directed against the Kantian finitude for which our nature entails that intuition can only ever be sensuous; it requires subjecting intuitivity itself to an essential enlargement against its Kantian sense, so that the concept in its categorial figure affects us and is given.

engagements.claim: Marion reads the breakthrough of the Investigations through Nietzsche's late fragment 'How I recognise my own kind': intuition without remainder answers Zarathustra's unlimited Yes, so that Nietzsche, accomplishing the metaphysics of presence, would recognise Husserl as his own kind.
engagements.quote: To accomplish the metaphysics of presence, Nietzsche can therefore recognise as his strangest and most unavoidable own kind — Husserl.

engagements.claim: Against Derrida, Marion shows that Husserl himself criticises as non-phenomenological, in Erdmann and Sigwart, the confusion of signification with fulfilling intuition that Derrida attributes to him, and that Derrida's key citation omits Husserl's own thesis.
engagements.quote: Husserl criticises as non-phenomenological the confusion Derrida attributes to him, in an anachronism as exemplary as it is ideal.

engagements.claim: Marion confirms Derrida's conclusion that the Investigations fall under the metaphysics of presence but contests his principal argument: by supposing that signification breaks with presence, Derrida exempts it from metaphysics, because his concept of presence is too narrow to reach givenness.
engagements.quote: Derrida's reading is paradoxically not radical enough, since by supposing signification to break with presence he exempts it from metaphysics, and he does so because his understanding of presence is too narrow to reach its properly Husserlian deepening as givenness

engagements.claim: Husserl never asks in the Investigations what givenness means; leaving uninterrogated the givenness he enlarged, he concedes Derrida's thesis and keeps givenness in metaphysical detention under presence.
engagements.quote: His silence amounts to conceding Derrida's thesis: leaving uninterrogated the givenness whose enlargement he has nevertheless carried out, Husserl does not free it from the bolt of presence and so keeps it in metaphysical detention.

engagements.claim: Marion credits Heidegger with seeing that the breakthrough consists in the enlargement of givenness beyond sensuous intuition and with inheriting Husserl by asking what givenness means, without reducing it too soon to presence.
engagements.quote: Heidegger, seeing at once with extraordinary lucidity that the breakthrough consists wholly in the enlargement of givenness beyond sensuous intuition, assumes the Husserlian inheritance exactly by bearing his whole interrogation on what such givenness means, and by guarding against reducing it too soon to presence, even under the figure of categorial intuition.

engagements.claim: Heidegger's first turn contests Husserl's prohibition of ontology while remaining occupied with the articulation of phenomenology and ontology at the end of the Ideas: phenomenology becomes method by displacing its matter from entities to being.
engagements.quote: Even in its parricide, Heidegger's first turn stays faithfully occupied with the last word of the *Ideas*: the articulation of phenomenology and ontology.

engagements.claim: Measured by Heidegger's criterion of the phenomenological, the mode of exhibiting phenomena, Husserl's phenomenology remains non-phenomenological, phenomenological only in intention, because it diverts intentionality and the reduction to the ideal of an absolute science.
engagements.quote: Measured against the criterion of the phenomenological — considering not phenomena but the mode of their exhibition — the conclusion, however violent the paradox, is that Husserl's phenomenology remains non-phenomenological, phenomenological only in intention and not yet in a fundamental and principial sense.

engagements.claim: For intentionality and the reduction, the two acquisitions Husserl then diverts toward an absolute science, Heidegger always acknowledges himself Husserl's disciple.
engagements.quote: Husserl does not follow phenomenology's guiding thread to its terminus, the question of being, because having won intentionality and the reduction — for which Heidegger always acknowledges himself his disciple — he diverts them to accomplish the philosophical ideal of an absolute science of and through consciousness.

engagements.claim: Husserl does not respect the return to the things themselves, because in the Ideas it competes with the principle of all principles, which makes originarily giving intuition the source of right before any reduction.
engagements.quote: Husserl does not respect it — not merely because Heidegger says so, but because in the *Ideas* that principle competes with another, exceptionally titled the principle of all principles

engagements.claim: Heidegger's § 7 keeps Husserl's phenomenon as what shows itself in itself but draws from its non-showings the opposite of a reduction to presence: coveredness is the counter-concept of phenomenon, and the phenomenon is ringed with inapparence.
engagements.quote: From the deviant senses of the self-showing, that is from the phenomenon's non-showings, Heidegger draws not the need for a drastic reduction to presence absolutely given for consciousness but the opposite conclusion: coveredness is the counter-concept to phenomenon.

engagements.claim: Marion rejects Husserl's verdict, to Ingarden and in the 1930 Afterword, that Heidegger misunderstood the reduction; Husserl sees only one reduction where Heidegger relaunches it a second time, from the entity to its being.
engagements.quote: Marion therefore rejects Husserl's verdict to Ingarden that Heidegger grasped neither this path nor the whole sense of the method of reduction

engagements.claim: In the 1923/24 course that became First Philosophy, and already in the 1907 Göttingen lectures, Husserl expounds and approves Descartes, whose genius sowed the seeds of transcendental philosophy.
engagements.quote: At the very moment Heidegger was expounding and criticising Descartes at Marburg, Husserl was expounding and approving him at Freiburg, in the winter 1923/24 course that became *First Philosophy*: even when he happened to hold a false theory, Descartes' philosophical genius led him to sow the seeds of transcendental philosophy.

engagements.claim: Citing Descartes' definition of substance to fix the being of consciousness, Husserl drops alia from alia re and puts res in quotation marks, so as not to make consciousness a res while opposing it to reality.
engagements.quote: (c) Husserl modifies the formula: he drops *alia* from *alia re* and accepts *res* only in quotation marks.

engagements.claim: Heidegger distances himself from Husserl by criticising the Cartesian presuppositions within his phenomenology: the critique of Descartes is aimed first and equally at Husserl, who is the less a phenomenologist the more he remains a Cartesian.
engagements.quote: Descartes will undergo a critique that is aimed first and equally at Husserl, who is the less a phenomenologist the more he remains a Cartesian.

engagements.claim: In Sein und Zeit Descartes' first failure is the total ontological indeterminacy of the res cogitans: he examined the cogitare of the ego but left the sum unelucidated.
engagements.quote: That indeterminacy marks Descartes' first and radical failure: a total ontological indeterminacy of the *res cogitans sive mens sive animus*

engagements.claim: Correcting Heidegger as a historian, Marion notes that Descartes attributes permanence first to the ego, reduced to what remains certain, before the res extensa that Heidegger cites.
engagements.quote: The reference is exact, but it masks another that attributes permanence first and directly to the *ego* before the *res extensa*

engagements.claim: The kinship of Cartesian finitude with Dasein stays masked to Heidegger, who sees the ego's finitude only through ancient-Christian anthropology and reduces finite and infinite substance to efficient production.
engagements.quote: The pertinence of the comparison stays masked to and by Heidegger, who envisages the *ego*'s finitude only within the horizon of ancient-Christian anthropology and reduces the relation between finite and infinite substance to efficient production, so as to deny Cartesian finitude any originary validity.

engagements.claim: Heidegger destroys the Cartesian ego and yet retranscribes the analytic of Dasein in its displaced terms ('I am', mineness, indebtedness): between ego and Dasein the struggle is over the interpretation of one and the same phenomenon.
engagements.quote: Between *ego* and Dasein, Descartes and Heidegger, what is at stake beyond the patent critique is a struggle for the interpretation of one and the same phenomenon — "I think," "I am."

engagements.claim: Heidegger's ontological difference recovers the difference of manners of being between consciousness and reality fixed in Ideas I § 42, and parts from Husserl by thinking as ontological a difference Husserl named but left indeterminate.
engagements.quote: Heidegger does not separate himself from Husserl by introducing an ontological difference Husserl ignored, but by radically deepening as ontological a difference of essence and manner of being that Husserl left indeterminate as such.

engagements.claim: Sein und Zeit cannot found access to the sense of being on Dasein, which lets only the being of entities be read; to attribute to Dasein the manifestation of the sense of being confuses the two gaps of the question, as § 83 and Heidegger's own marginalia concede.
engagements.quote: To attribute to Dasein the direct manifestation of the sense of being is therefore first to confuse the two moments and gaps of the question of being, and second to overvalue Dasein's reach arbitrarily — as the aporia of §83 confirms.

engagements.claim: Heidegger in 1925 refuses Husserl's 1912 separation of ontology from phenomenology: there is no ontology alongside a phenomenology, and scientific ontology is phenomenology; the opposition made his divergence from Husserl possible and necessary before 1927.
engagements.quote: Heidegger in 1925: there is no ontology alongside a phenomenology; scientific ontology is nothing other than phenomenology. Husserl in 1912: in itself, ontology is not phenomenology.

engagements.claim: Marion turns Husserl's demand for phenomenological intelligibility of every ontology against any later attempt to restore classical ontology, even by destroying it, and aims the objection at Sein und Zeit.
engagements.quote: the demand for phenomenological intelligibility of whatever ontology claims to treat will press all the harder on any subsequent attempt to restore classical ontology — even by destroying it. Marion is already aiming that remark at *Sein und Zeit*.

engagements.claim: Marion credits Heidegger, from the threefold structure of the question named in the 1925 course, with a reduction redoubled: from the entity to the being of entities, then from the being of entities to the sense of being.
engagements.quote: That formal result suffices for understanding Heidegger's own practice of the reduction, which sets itself to question to the bottom — that is, in two moments, relaunching the entity twice rather than once.

engagements.claim: Heidegger keeps intentionality as the ratio cognoscendi of Dasein's transcendence, but intentionality thought to its root implies being-in-the-world, which Marion marks as another line of fracture with Husserl.
engagements.quote: intentionality is the *ratio cognoscendi* of transcendence. Intentionality thought to its root implies a world, more exactly being-in-the-world — another line of fracture with Husserl

engagements.claim: Against the charge of anthropology, Marion defends Dasein's privilege as strictly phenomenological, while finding Sein und Zeit more reticent than the 1925 course in saying so.
engagements.quote: It is not enough to say, with *Sein und Zeit* — which Marion finds more reticent here — that understanding of being is itself a determination of Dasein's being

engagements.claim: Marion reads the 1929 lecture's anxiety as a second, generalised implementation of the redoubled reduction, exercised on entities in their totality rather than on Dasein alone, and leading them back to being.
engagements.quote: Anxiety thereby performs a phenomenological reduction by leading entities in totality back to being.

engagements.claim: In the 1929 reduction being is reached as the accomplishment of a movement of referral, not as what remains after the entity founders: not, in Husserl's idiom, as a residue.
engagements.quote: being is not discovered as the last piece of flotsam of the entity's sepulchral shipwreck, nor, in Husserl's idiom, as a residue.

engagements.claim: Heidegger rejects Husserl's reduction as non-phenomenological while relaunching it, by phenomenology's method and the principle of return to the things themselves, toward being as phenomenon; he neither abandons nor refutes Husserl.
engagements.quote: at the very moment he rejects and claims to overstep Husserl's reduction as non-phenomenological, Heidegger can still legitimately call himself Husserl's disciple

engagements.claim: Marion grants Heidegger phenomenology's second breakthrough, after the Logical Investigations: intentionality returned to the being of entities, so that ontological difference defines the breakthrough entirely; but the breakthrough stands or falls with how the difference is attested.
engagements.quote: It accomplishes a second when Heidegger assigns intentionality to return, as to the matter itself, no longer to entities but to their being.

engagements.claim: Marion dismantles the conclusion, drawn from Heidegger's 1949 foreword to Vom Wesen des Grundes, that ontological difference is named only in 1928/29 and is foreign to Sein und Zeit.
engagements.quote: That conclusion, however widely accepted, is on examination extremely fragile, and Marion dismantles it in three moves.

engagements.claim: The summer 1927 course names ontological difference at § 22, but Marion asks whether it is won there or only programmed: the second part breaks off after one chapter, and the difference is recognised as an unanswered aporia.
engagements.quote: One may even ask whether, named here, ontological difference is really won at all — whether this is a record of phenomenological victory or a programme for a breakthrough still to be made.

engagements.claim: Marion refuses Beaufret's formula that Sein und Zeit is the book of the difference of being and entities although the word does not yet come forward, as an explanation that itself demands explanation.
engagements.quote: Marion refuses the formula as an explanation demanding an explanation: how is one to understand that the book of the difference of being and entities is precisely the one that keeps completely silent about its locution and its word?

engagements.claim: Against the commentators, Marion finds the phrase ontological difference used in Sein und Zeit (§ 12, § 63), worked verbally at § 2 and the end of Division One, and confirmed by Heidegger's marginalia: the 1927 breakthrough is accomplished within ontological difference.
engagements.quote: First point: Heidegger does use the phrase "ontological difference" in *Sein und Zeit*, contrary to the commentators' opinion, so far as Marion knows without exception.

engagements.claim: The acknowledgements credit Courtine and Franck with a practice of phenomenology older and better than Marion's own, placing the book within the French Husserl scholarship of the Paris Archives.
engagements.quote: Courtine and Franck are credited with a practice of phenomenology older and better than his own
